title: What does 'fair value' look like in practice? Three years into the Consumer Duty, here’s what we’ve learned.
raw_summary: Fair value is a simple yet important principle at the heart of the Consumer Duty: the price customers pay should be reasonable, relative to the benefits they get. But applying that principle in practice requires judgement.Three years into the Consumer Duty, we’re seeing clear differences between firms that have embedded fair value into their approach and those that still need to strengthen their assessments, evidence and monitoring.We recently reviewed how firms across the consumer finance market assess, evidence and monitor fair value. We also carried out focused work on fees and charges across a range of credit products, and supervisory work on consumer hire and third-party ownership agreements for home energy infrastructure.Many firms are getting it right, building fair value into how they design, price and monitor their products. Others are missing things that, in hindsight, could have been avoidable. Where firms fell short, a recurring issue was the evidence supporting their conclusions.Here are 3 areas that separated the 2, and questions firms can use to challenge their approach to assessing and monitoring fair value.Does your evidence actually tell you something, or just describe your product?Across the firms and products we reviewed, stronger fair value assessments showed a clear, evidenced relationship between what customers paid and the benefits they could reasonably expect to receive. One credit card provider, for example, quantified the cashback, foreign exchange savings and other account benefits customers received, and set these directly against the fees and interest they paid. That gave them a clear evidence base for their fair value conclusion, not just a description of the product's features.Weaker assessments tended to rely on assumptions rather than actual customer data. Some had relevant evidence, but it was scattered across different documents and never brought together into a coherent picture. This made it hard for anyone, including us, to see how firms had reached their conclusions.Are you assessing fair value for different customer groups?Fair value isn't one-size-fits-all. Firms showing an understanding of that nuance segmented their customers by factors such as credit risk, product usage, distribution channel and characteristics of vulnerability, and assessed fair value across the resulting groups. Some firms also assessed fair value across different pricing groups, including APR bands and risk-based pricing groups, to understand whether customers paying different prices continued to receive fair value. Other firms treated their whole target market as a single, homogeneous group when testing fair value. This made it difficult to spot if some customers were quietly paying more, or getting less, than others, which is exactly the kind of thing a fair value assessment is supposed to identify.If customers can't picture the real cost, does the price even matter?Fair value also needs to be considered alongside customer understanding. Even a well-designed, fairly priced product can fall short if customers don't understand what they're signing up to. Some firms tested comprehension directly, including one that proactively contacted customers incurring certain charges to check they understood how and when those charges applied. This gave the firm evidence about whether customers understood the charges, rather than relying only on the existence or readability of disclosures.We also looked at consumer hire agreements for home energy equipment, where some promotions used 'pay as you save' claims that could lead customers to believe that savings or affordability were guaranteed. Those outcomes depended on factors such as equipment performance, changes in customers’ circumstances and future energy prices over agreements lasting up to 25 years. Firms should make these clear and avoid creating the impression that savings or affordability are assured.What this means for your firm Use these findings to challenge your approach to assessing and monitoring fair value. Ask:Does your evidence tell you something meaningful about customer outcomes, or does it simply describe your product?Does your target market behave as one group once you look closely?Can customers understand the total price they might pay and the financial commitment they are entering into?A common feature of stronger approaches was that firms supported their conclusions with evidence rather than relying on assumptions.The good news is that this doesn’t need to always require complex modelling or new data. Smaller firms may be able to draw on information they already hold, including complaints, arrears, customer feedback and product usage.If there's one thing to take from this, it's to show your working: what your evidence shows, how it supports your conclusion, what you'd do if it didn't.We expect firms to read the full findings. They also cover how firms assessed total price and benefits, used competitor benchmarking, and used controls to reduce the risk of foreseeable harm from fees and charges, including the home energy sector examples we touched on above.We'll keep monitoring this area through our supervisory work and will continue sharing what we learn as our understanding develops.

title: FCA stops HTX's crypto promotions
raw_summary: The FCA has secured High Court undertakings to ensure that HTX (formerly Huobi), a global crypto exchange, will not knowingly promote cryptoasset services unlawfully to UK consumers. The FCA took legal action against HTX in October 2025 for breaking UK financial promotion rules. HTX had failed repeatedly to engage with the FCA. Following the commencement of proceedings, HTX took steps to exit the UK. The FCA and Huobi Global S.A. have now reached a settlement in the case. HTX is no longer active in the UK. Consumers can no longer make deposits, and new UK users cannot sign up to the platform. HTX will not target, solicit or actively seek to engage UK consumers.UK users of HTX should read the information published on HTX's website about the availability of its services in the UK and the arrangements for withdrawing any residual assets.Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said: 'Crypto firms should be under no illusion: being based overseas does not put them beyond the reach of UK law. Our action means HTX is leaving the UK and can no longer target UK consumers. The message to other firms is clear: follow the rules or face the consequences.'Consumers should check a firm's permissions using the FCA Firm Checker and remember that cryptoassets are high-risk investments.Notes to editorsRead details of the proceedings and relevant court documents. Huobi Global S.A. is the first defendant in the proceedings.View the court order (PDF) containing the undertakings. Huobi Global's undertakings to the court include that it will not knowingly, directly or indirectly, communicate or cause to be communicated a financial promotion in contravention of section 21 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000. This covers the HTX website, software applications and social media platforms.The proceedings were commenced in the Business and Property Division of the High Court on 21 October 2025.The FCA publicly announced its enforcement action on 10 February 2026. The terms of the settlement are confidential. The settlement does not constitute an admission of liability or wrongdoing by Huobi Global or any other person or entity.Crypto is a high-risk investment and remains largely unregulated in the UK, except for anti-money laundering and financial promotions until October 2027. Use the FCA Firm Checker to check a firm’s permissions.

title: Defence SMEs need banking services that work
raw_summary: The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusionThe current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.Defence is not one-size-fits-allThere is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.Better information leads to better decisionsAnother theme that stood out was the importance of data.Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:Are applications taking longer than expected?Are decisions being applied consistently?Do governance processes reflect actual risk?Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.Getting the balance rightOur work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.Read our findings.

title: FCA calls on private market firms to manage conflicts of interest in line with rapid growth
raw_summary: Private market firms vary in how well they identify and manage conflicts of interest, according to an FCA review. Private markets refer to investments in assets, companies, or debt not listed or traded on public exchanges. They’ve grown significantly in recent years, and the UK is a leading international centre. Private markets play an increasingly important role in providing capital to businesses and opportunities for returns to investors. Private markets can give rise to conflicts that differ from those in public markets, and effective disclosure is important to enable investors to assess whether their interests are being protected.The FCA found examples of good practice by firms across private equity, private credit and real estate asset classes. These included strong governance arrangements, effective oversight and independent challenge. It also identified some areas where firms could strengthen governance, oversight and conflicts management arrangements to support fair investor outcomes.As private markets grow and business models become more complex, the FCA found that some firms were failing to identify conflicts adequately or keep their controls up to date. Recurring weaknesses were identified in areas including cross-fund transfers and multi-party transactions, gifts and entertainment, and information barriers.The FCA expects firms to be able to identify, record, manage and disclose conflicts effectively, and demonstrate that investors are being treated fairly, particularly in areas where investors place significant reliance on firms' judgement, governance and controls.Michelle Beck, director of wholesale buy-side at the FCA, said: 'Firms need to ensure their management of conflicts of interest keeps pace with growth in their size and complexity. We found good practice across the sector, but standards varied considerably. We want to encourage confidence in the UK’s private markets. Firms should act on our findings and identify where they can strengthen controls.'Although not part of this review, the FCA is examining governance and conflicts concerns relating to the use of private credit to fund consumer litigation claims, including significant risks of harm to investors, consumers and markets.Notes to editorsConflicts of interest and fair customer treatment in private markets.The review examined how firms identify, manage, mitigate and disclose conflicts of interest across private equity, private credit and real estate markets.The report includes examples of both good practice and areas where firms could strengthen arrangements.The review forms part of the FCA's wider supervisory focus on private markets and investor outcomes.

title: Beyond borders: Regulating the risks we share
raw_summary: Speech by Ashley Alder, FCA Chair, at the Michael D. Gill Lecture on International Financial Regulatory Understanding and Cooperation. I wasn’t fortunate enough to work as closely with Mike as many of you in this room.But I knew him well enough during my time with the IOSCO board to appreciate someone who was kind and unassuming, whilst being absolutely determined to make lives better through his work.He personified the very best attributes of dedicated public service.In his 2024 lecture Andrew Bailey described Mike as a passionate internationalist, and reflected on what this meant for the UK after the Brexit referendum.Two years on, the values that Mike championed are even more on point.Mike understood implicitly that relationships between regulators are about so much more than institutional goodwill – they depend on trust, candour and constructive practical action.That’s an aspect of his legacy that is just as relevant – perhaps even more so – today.In an increasingly interconnected global financial system, no institution can see the whole picture on its own.Success depends not only on what each regulator does individually, but on what we can see, understand, test, and address together.

title: FCA restricts 6 firms following concerns over anti-money laundering controls
raw_summary: Restrictions have been placed on 6 unregulated lenders, known as Annex 1 firms, after the FCA raised concerns about their anti-money laundering policies, controls and procedures while assessing their applications. The restrictions were imposed by the FCA on each firm’s request and limit their ability to take on new customers or do new business with existing customers, including extending existing credit.This action forms part of the FCA’s enhanced oversight of Annex 1 firms. These firms operate in sectors that can present a heightened risk of money laundering and other financial crime and are required to register with the FCA for supervision under the Money Laundering Regulations. They are not authorised or subject to wider FCA regulation.The FCA has previously warned Annex 1 firms that they will be subject to increased scrutiny. They must be able to demonstrate they understand the financial crime risks they face and have effective systems and controls in place to manage those risks, or face action.More widely, the FCA is assessing responses to an information request sent to around 900 registered Annex 1 firms to identify and disrupt financial crime risks and determine where further action is needed.The FCA has also reminded regulated firms that, when dealing with Annex 1 firms, they must carry out due diligence to understand the firm’s business, in accordance with legislative requirements. This includes seeking direct confirmation from the firm of its registration status, conducting independent checks of the information it provides, and understanding and managing any risks.Registration under the Money Laundering Regulations is not a substitute for regulated firms carrying out their own appropriate due diligence.Steve Smart, executive director lead for fighting financial crime at the FCA, said: 'We have warned Annex 1 firms that they face increased scrutiny. They must demonstrate they can manage the money laundering risks they face. Where they cannot satisfy us, we will intervene.'Notes to editorsVoluntary restrictions were imposed on Kingscrown Finance Ltd on 21 April 2026, with further voluntary restrictions imposed on 25 September 2026. The further restrictions limit how Kingscrown may receive payments from existing customers and require an orderly wind-down of its existing loan book.On 7 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on MOMSB Ltd and Momentus Capital Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements subject to limited exceptions, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.On 9 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Grosvenor Funding Ltd and Grosvenor Funding (North West) Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.On 15 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Abbital Ltd. The restrictions specify the circumstances in which Abbital may take on new customers, enter into new lending arrangements or accept payments from existing customers. They also require an independent review of Abbital’s anti-money laundering systems and controls.Fighting financial crime is one of the FCA's strategic priorities.

title: Reshaping regulation, deliberately
raw_summary: Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026. Reform: more than writing rulesIn this sector, we’re just past peak rule making. The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.But we’re not done yet.We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.It takes a strategic approach. title: Former chief executive banned after misconduct led to £4m losses in high-risk investments
raw_summary: The FCA has banned Jeffrey Dawkins, the former chief executive of Vector Wealth Ltd, after he dishonestly acted as a front for a disqualified director using the company to sell high-risk bonds. Mr Dawkins has also been fined nearly £270,000.In 2019, Mr Dawkins sold Vector Wealth to a disqualified director who described himself as CEO and wanted to use Vector Wealth’s FCA-authorised status to sell mini-bonds.Mr Dawkins told the FCA he was still in charge, but the new “CEO” was really running the firm. This deception allowed the disqualified director to promote mini-bonds using the legitimacy of the firm to make them appear safer than they were.The disqualified director and Kadir Kanizi, a former senior manager at Vector Wealth, promoted the bonds but investors were not properly warned about the risks.Investors put in £105,000 on average, with one investing £1.1 million. Before seeing the marketing material, they had to confirm they were high net worth or sophisticated investors. Investors are expected to lose about £4 million.The FCA has banned Mr Kanizi from senior management roles. He was fined for failing to make sure consumers were properly warned about the risks.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said, 'Jeffrey Dawkins acted as a front man for a banned director, helping high-risk investments look safer than they were.'Mr Dawkins and Mr Kanizi allowed misleading promotions to draw in investors, many of whom now face significant losses. Mini-bonds and similar investments are very high risk, and people should be extremely cautious.'The FCA has warned about the risks of investing in mini-bonds and loan notes. A loan note or mini-bond usually involves lending money to a company for a set period in return for interest. If that company fails, consumers could lose every penny.Consumers need to be alert to the risk of harm and protect themselves using the tools available, like the FCA Firm Checker.Notes to editorsRead the final notices for Jeffrey Dawkins and Kadir Kanizi.There is statutory obligation to report the change in control of authorised firms.Vector Wealth Limited was formed as Fifth Quarter Asset Management (UK) Limited on 23 March 2012. Mr Dawkins held authorised positions at the firm from 5 March 2013. Vector Wealth’s authorisation ended on 28 January 2025.Mr Kanizi was appointed as a director on 22 September 2020 and was approved by the FCA on 6 September 2021.The disqualified director was banned from acting as a company director for 12 years in August 2014.The penalty in respect of Mr Dawkins includes a multiplier to reflect the seriousness of the conduct. It also includes an uplift for failing to cooperate with the FCA’s investigation. The full calculation is set out at section 6 of the Final Notice. Mr Dawkins has also been ordered to pay £57,298 plus interest (£68,257) of the proceeds he received from selling Vector Wealth and continuing to act as its director and approved person.The FCA has calculated that Kadir Kanizi should have been fined £80,096 but it reduced the penalty to £20,000 after he demonstrated that it would cause serious financial hardship. In the interest of maximising the funds available to be distributed to investors, the FCA agreed not to enforce the penalty if the same amount was made available by Mr Kanizi to Vector Wealth’s liquidators. He has also agreed to complete consumer duty training before taking up any future role in financial services.Investors who bought bonds through Vector Wealth should contact the firm’s liquidator and check the FCA website for updates.The FCA has investigated the matters that fall within its remit. The FCA may share relevant information with other law enforcement agencies where appropriate. Confirming or comment on individual referrals could risk affecting ongoing investigations.The FCA now actively removes the unutilised permissions of firms. Historically firms were expected to voluntarily request cancellation of unused permissions.The FCA permanently banned the marketing of speculative illiquid securities, including mini-bonds and loan notes, to retail investors from 1 January 2021.Anyone approached about loan notes, mini-bonds or similar high-risk investments should stop and check before investing, especially where adverts promise big, fixed returns or make the investment look simple and safe. Use the FCA’s Firm Checker and Warning List before handing over any money.

title: Three arrests in major FCA operation against criminal insider dealing ring

title: Two plead guilty after clients lose £2m in fraud case
raw_summary: Two people who worked at financial advice firms have pleaded guilty to fraud after 4 clients lost £2m. raw_summary: sycl : vectorize reordered-layout dequantization stores (Q4_0, K-quants, IQ3, MXFP4) ( #30976 ) sycl : widen reordered q4_0 dequantization stores The reordered-layout Q4_0 conversion kernel processed one qs byte per work-item with two scalar stores, strided 16 elements apart. Give it the same treatment the Q8_0 kernel got in #30775 : a flat sycl::range<1> launch with four qs bytes (8 outputs) per work-item inside one 32-element block and two vec<dst_t,4> stores. Same float math and rounding as the scalar kernel; output is bit-identical. The existing k % QK4_0 == 0 assert guarantees whole 32-element blocks, so the k/8 launch covers every row exactly. The now-unreferenced scalar reorder kernel is removed. Arc Pro B70, primed prefill (prefill after decode on a reorder-installed tensor): +6.4% to +7.3% pp512/pp2048 on Q4_0 models (tested up to 27B dense); fresh-layout prefill and decode unchanged; PPL within run noise. sycl : vectorize reordered q4_K dequantization stores The reordered-layout Q4_K conversion kernel already loads its quantized inputs through sycl::vec but writes the dequantized results with scalar stores. Build the results in a vec<dst_t,n> register and emit two vector stores instead. Same per-element math; output is bit-identical. Arc Pro B70, primed prefill (prefill after decode on a reorder-installed tensor): +14.7% to +15.3% pp512/pp2048 on Q4_K-dominant models (tested up to 27B dense); fresh-layout prefill, decode and PPL unchanged. sycl : remap reordered q5_K dequantization to vec4 loads/stores The reordered-layout Q5_K conversion kernel gave each thread only four outputs fed by scalar ql/qh byte loads plus a local-memory scale broadcast, so the stores were never its bottleneck: widening the stores alone measured within noise on mixed-quant models and +0.5% on a q5_K-dominant model. Re-decompose to 32 threads per block, each consuming four consecutive ql and qh bytes and emitting two aligned vec<dst_t,4> stores; a 4-element run shares one scale pair, so the per-element math and the output are identical. Arc Pro B70, primed prefill on a q5_K-dominant 27B model: +3.6% pp512/pp2048 over the scalar kernel; fresh-layout prefill, decode and PPL unchanged. The GET_ROWS reorder path moves to the same 32-thread decomposition. sycl : remap reordered q6_K dequantization to vec4 stores The reordered-layout Q6_K conversion kernel wrote four scalars per thread, strided 32 elements apart, each pair of neighbors sharing neither instruction stream nor store transaction. Re-decompose the same 64-thread work-group so each thread emits one aligned vec<dst_t,4>: a 4-element run shares one 16-element scale group, one ql nibble source and one qh bit pair, so the per-element math and the output are identical to the scalar kernel. Arc Pro B70, primed prefill: +28.7% pp512/pp2048 on a Q6_K 27B model; fresh-layout prefill, decode and PPL unchanged. sycl : vectorize reordered q3_K dequantization stores Each thread of the reordered-layout Q3_K conversion kernel already computes four consecutive outputs; build them in a vec<dst_t,4> register and emit one vector store instead of four scalars. Same per-element math; output is bit-identical.
